summary:
P.A.N.D.U: A Way Through Gale is a Planetary Atmospheric, Navigation & Diagnostic Unit for Mars astronauts: a wrist-worn, layered map of the terrain around them. Its main readout is one number, the minutes the astronaut can spare before they must be under cover. That number is whichever runs out first, oxygen, battery or radiation dose budget, minus the walking time to shelter. The map shows slope hazards and rock types and routes around terrain too steep to cross, while other tabs track weather, dust and radiation.

We built it on an 18.2 x 15.1 km slice of Mount Sharp in Gale Crater from archived NASA data: Mars Trek terrain, Curiosity REMS weather, RAD radiation, Mastcam dust opacity and the Gale rock-type map. High on the slope, thinner air cuts modeled radiation shielding by up to nearly half, so the same walk costs more dose.

We replay the real 2018 dust storm, when opacity climbed from 0.76 to 7.94, and add modeled failures: a suit leak and a Solar Particle Event. The sector lies about 49 km from Curiosity’s landing site, outside its 20 km safe traverse radius, so the shelters are simulated.
details:
P.A.N.D.U: A Way Through Gale (Planetary Atmospheric, Navigation & Diagnostic Unit) is a first-person and third-person Mars EVA survival simulation set on an 18.2 by 15.1 km sector of Mount Sharp's southern slope inside the 154 km Gale Crater. Running from archived and created using NASA datasets , it models astronaut traversal roughly 49 km away from Curiosity's northeastern landing site, where thinner air cuts natural radiation shielding nearly in half compared to the crater floor. After an opening animation where the astronaut checks glove seals and taps the forearm unit awake, users interact with an 8-tab wrist display (Map, Radiation, Environment, Suit, Event, Geology, Navigation, and System). Under Martian gravity (3.71 m/s²), walking speed follows Tobler's hiking function while background Dijkstra pathfinding evaluates a smoothed 400 by 400 grid to calculate a live Safe Margin across oxygen, radiation dose, and battery reserves, dynamically rerouting around steep cliffs during hazards.

The project is built around three pillars: Simulation, Education, and Implementation. For Simulation, NASA Mars Trek topography is paired with 4,745 sols of Curiosity REMS daily weather, Mastcam dust optical depth (including the 2018 dust storm), and Curiosity RAD radiation baselines (0.64 mSv/sol) to drive day-night Sol cycles, dust fog, and accelerated battery drain during severe nighttime cold. For Education, users toggle a Mars Odyssey THEMIS false-color orbital layer to compare mineral zones such as windblown dust, olivine-rich basalt, and summit exposures, and scan waypoints to inspect Martian regolith components including silicates, iron oxides, water-bearing clays, sulfates, and perchlorates. For Implementation, everything runs in a standalone Windows executable (mars.exe) built in Unity without cloud APIs or LLMs, featuring hyperlocalized 2D and 3D terrain maps, a ground-projected Terrain Scanner, and seeded A/B testing. Its primary benefit and intended impact is serving as an accessible educational sandbox that quantifies how autonomous offline telemetry reduces oxygen loss, radiation exposure, and steep-slope incidents when Earth communication is delayed.

PANDU uses multi-threaded pathfinding, barometric elevation models, and custom terrain derived from NASA Daataset and RenderTexture shaders built around archived NASA Trek, REMS, Mastcam, RAD, and THEMIS datasets.
